Mozart, Haydn and Beethoven used it sparingly to imitate Turkish military music; the earliest notation is in Gluck's operas Der betrogene Kadi and La Cythère Assiégée, and Liszt gives it a solo in the third movement of his Piano Concerto No. 1. It is also used in the wedding chorus of Wagner's Lohengrin, the third movement of Brahms's Symphony No. 4 and the opening of Lortzing's opera Der Waffenschmied. In Cajun music it marks the strong beats; Brazilian forró uses it with accordion and zabumba; in Indonesia it plays in the gendér and the gamelan.

The triangle is an idiophone of the percussion family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.211. A metal rod is bent into a triangle with one corner left open, and it is usually hung on a cord or wire so that it vibrates freely, then struck with a metal beater. In theory it has no fixed pitch, and a strike produces rich overtones. The player can hold it or clip it to a stand and use a finger to damp it and control volume and colour; complex rhythms can be played on a stand with two beaters. It is used in the European classical orchestra and opera, and also in folk and popular music such as forró, Cajun and rock; in Indonesia it plays with the gamelan in the gendér, and it is used in the rites of the Coptic and Malankara churches.
三角鐵的歷史主要來自圖像資料。有學者認為它源自古埃及叉鈴，也有學者只視其與叉鈴有: The history of the triangle comes mainly from pictorial sources. Some scholars hold that it comes from the ancient Egyptian sistrum, while others see only a connection with the sistrum. Early images show it used in religious settings, such as the rites of the Coptic Church in Egypt and the Malankara Church in Kerala, India. From the fourteenth century the triangle appears in Western European Christian imagery, in shapes including the open corner, the closed corner, curved sides, trapezoid and stirrup forms, some with small rings hung on them. In 1589 a list of the Württemberg court musicians in Germany writes the name "triangle" for the first time. After the eighteenth century European opera and orchestral composers borrowed it to imitate the metallic sound and rhythm of Turkish military music; in the nineteenth century Romantic composers prized its long sustain, which put the small rings out of use.
三角鐵的發聲體為金屬棒彎成三角形，一端留有開口。來源提及可用鋁、鈹銅、黃銅、青銅: The sounding body of the triangle is a metal rod bent into a triangle with one corner left open. The sources mention aluminium, beryllium copper, brass, bronze, iron and steel, and modern instruments are mostly steel or brass. It is usually hung on a cord or wire, often nylon fishing line, so that the body vibrates freely, and struck with a metal beater. The open end once carried a decorative scroll, which modern instruments no longer use. The sources do not state the materials of the other parts.
三角鐵的音色清亮透徹，具有穿透力強的特質。其聲音明亮刺激，帶有金屬質感的冷冽光澤: The triangle's tone is clear and bright and carries well. The sound is brilliant and piercing, with the cool sheen of metal; it sits in the high frequency range and cuts through the sound of a whole orchestra. Because of the hollow triangular shape and the metal, a strike produces rich overtones and a resonance of its own, and the sound hangs and lingers. Beside the heavy blur of large cymbals the triangle seems nimble and fine; beside the depth and solemnity of a bell it is light and lively. A single stroke is crisp and short, good for precise punctuation; repeated strokes make a continuous, glittering high-frequency sound that heightens the drama and the visual effect of a piece.
三角鐵通常以線或金屬絲穿過頂端彎曲處懸掛，使琴體自由振動；初學時先以敲棒敲擊，再: The triangle is usually hung by a cord or wire through the bend at the top so that the body vibrates freely; a beginner first strikes it with the beater, then touches the body lightly with the hand holding the clip to damp it or change the colour. For more complex, fast rhythms it can be fixed to a stand with two clips and played with two beaters, though that is harder to control. For a very soft sound, use a lighter beater or a knitting needle; a wooden beater gives a different tone. In a roll, the beater moves quickly back and forth between the two sides of the upper or lower corner. In folk music the triangle can also be held in the hand, with a finger pressed on one side to change the tone, and the sound adjusted by altering the striking point and by fine damping.
